claim: The requirement says MessagePack attributes on T must be honoured when present. With no SurrogateType, the collector always uses contractless mode. It never looks at [MessagePackObject]/[Key]/[IgnoreMember] or [DataContract]/[DataMember]/[IgnoreDataMember] on T. As a result, a member T marks [IgnoreMember] or [IgnoreDataMember] is still serialized under its name, and [Key(n)] integer keys are replaced by string name keys. That is both a wire-format mismatch with T's declared contract and an exposure of members the type author excluded.

claim: The change modifies MessagePackSecurity's hash-collision fallback so it returns EqualityComparer<T>.Default instead of throwing TypeAccessException. With UntrustedData, arbitrary key types now get non-collision-resistant comparers. This is unrelated to REQ-2129 (formatters for referenced types) and silently weakens secure-by-default deserialization, exposing hash-flooding DoS.

claim: Contractless mode here covers only public read-write members and requires an accessible parameterless constructor. The requirement asks for 'contractless behaviour over public members'. MessagePack's contractless resolver also serializes public get-only properties and deserializes through constructor parameters. A referenced type with get-only public properties, or only a parameterized constructor, either silently loses those members or is rejected with MsgPack007. That is narrower than contractless behaviour.

claim: A guard was removed. Under UntrustedData (HashCollisionResistant = true), a key type with no hash-resistant comparer used to throw TypeAccessException. It now silently falls back to EqualityComparer<T>.Default. Dictionaries and HashSets keyed by arbitrary user types become open to hash-flooding when deserializing untrusted data. Nothing in REQ-2129 asks for this. Input that breaks it: MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData.GetEqualityComparer<SomeUserClass>() returns a comparer instead of throwing.

claim: GeneratedFormatterCollector never reads MessagePack attributes on the formatted type T. It always uses contractless mode, or surrogate mode if a surrogate is given, so [MessagePackObject], [Key(n)], [IgnoreMember] and [DataContract]/[DataMember] on T are ignored. The acceptance criterion 'If T does carry MessagePack attributes, they are honoured' is not met. Example: T has [Key(0)] int Visible and [IgnoreMember] string IgnoredSecret. The generated formatter serializes both under string keys, which leaks the ignored member and is wire-incompatible with the int-key array layout the dynamic resolver produces.

claim: GetEqualityComparer fallback now returns EqualityComparer<T>.Default instead of throwing TypeAccessException for types with no hash-resistant comparer. This silently disables the hash-collision protection for UntrustedData, so existing secure users are no longer protected. It is unrelated to the requirement.

claim: Contractless members are ordered by name and given IntKey = index, but the string-key formatter is chosen with isIntKey=false. The wire format is then a map with sorted names, which differs from the dynamic ContractlessStandardResolver behaviour. Read-only properties, get-only members and private members are skipped, and members are not in declaration order. The emitted bytes may therefore not match what the dynamic contractless resolver produces for the same type.

receipt_plan.detail: Take a type with public properties declared out of alphabetical order. Serialize it with ContractlessStandardResolver and with the generated formatter, then compare the bytes. A mismatch in key order or in the omitted read-only members shows the drift.

claim: MessagePackSecurity.GetHashCollisionResistantEqualityComparer<T> no longer throws TypeAccessException for types without a known hash-resistant comparer. It now returns EqualityComparer<T>.Default, so with MessagePackSecurity.UntrustedData an attacker-controlled dictionary or hash-set key of any unlisted type uses a collision-prone comparer. This silently removes the hash-collision-resistance protection (hash-flooding DoS). It is unrelated to the formatter feature.
